([IATSE](https://iatse.net/strike-date-set-for-60000-film-and-television-workers/)) |
| **A5 WGA / SAG-AFTRA 2023** | **Confirmed as analogy** | The WGA's 2023 settlement included contractual restrictions on generative AI; SAG-AFTRA's 118-day strike ended with provisions covering digital replicas, including consent and compensation. Neither is VFX labor, as Sonnet correctly flagged. ([WGA](https://origin.www.wga.org/the-guild/about-us/history/a-history-of-wga-contract-negotiations-and-gains)) |
| **A6 longstanding VFX crunch** | **Confirmed through 2022/23; post-union trend not measurable yet** | A 2013 international VFX survey reported a typical “normal” week around **50 hours**, heavy weeks around **70**, and roughly **39% receiving no overtime compensation**. The IATSE 2022 survey later found 58% of client-side respondents and 39% of vendor-side respondents had worked uncompensated hours; its broader summary said 70% had experienced uncompensated overtime. That establishes persistence across roughly a decade. I found no comparable post-2025 measurement allowing the required 25%/10% change classification. ([Effects Corner](https://effectscorner.blogspot.com/2013/05/visual-effects-working-conditions-survey.html)) |

A1 gets even more interesting after Sonnet's cutoff. Marvel, Disney and Avatar VFX workers ratified first contracts in May 2025. The Marvel/Disney agreements explicitly added overtime, “pay for all hours worked,” rest/turnaround rules, meal penalties, minimum rates and roughly $13/hour in health/pension contributions. ([IATSE](https://","next_offset":4800}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":4800,"content":"iatse.net/iatse-vfx-members-overwhelmingly-ratify-first-three-contracts-with-major-studios-in-the-us/))

That is exceptionally relevant to the mechanism under study, but unfortunately for our little hypothesis cage match, it is **not Test A**, because organized labor changed at exactly the same time.

## 2. Variable extraction

This is where Sonnet's protocol starts savagely murdering otherwise tempting anecdotes, which is probably healthy.

| Variable | Best public evidence located | Result under the fixed dictionary |
|---|---|---|
| **H: overtime burden** | 2013 survey: ~50-hour normal week, ~70-hour heavy week; some NZ respondents reported 100-hour weeks. 2022 IATSE describes a 12-hour shoot as standard before pre/post-call work. | **Measurable only in some datasets; not consistently worker-project matched.** |
| **s: fraction of H transferred** | Surveys give the **fraction of workers** experiencing uncompensated work, not uncompensated hours ÷ total overtime hours. | **NOT FOUND.** Substituting “58% of workers” for Sonnet's `s` would violate its proxy rule. |
| **F: controller's non-transferable maintenance cost** | No public project-level studio accounting separating paid overtime, rework, penalties etc. | **UNMEASURABLE** for the cases examined. |
| **A: cost of alternative** | No comparable public bids showing “realistic schedule versus crunch schedule” in matched projects. | **UNMEASURABLE.** |
| **B: sustainable capacity threshold** | Strong qualitative health/burnout evidence, but no VFX dataset establishing “above X weekly hours attrition/sick leave increases.”","next_offset":6400}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":6400,"content":" | **UNMEASURABLE under the fixed definition.** |
| **R: replacement pool** | Evidence of global outsourcing and, in 2022, unusually high labor demand, but no clean VFX unemployment/labor-pool series matching the cases. | **NOT FOUND quantitatively.** |
| **O: organization** | Before 2023, IATSE described VFX as largely outside collective bargaining; discrete Marvel, Disney, Avatar and later units organized from 2023 onward. | **Qualitatively measurable, but sector-wide union density NOT FOUND.** |

One particularly useful money datapoint exists, though it cannot be paired cleanly with H: the 2022 IATSE survey reports client-side wage distributions. For example, median Data Wrangler compensation was reported as **$36.86/hour**, based on a modeled 60-hour week. But because the dataset does not supply a matched average number of *unpaid* hours for that role, calculating an unpaid-dollar burden would require inventing the missing input. So I did not. ([IATSE 2022 survey PDF](https://vfxunion.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2023/03/2022-VFX-IATSE-Rates-and-Conditions-Survey-FINAL.pdf))

## 3. Case records / discriminating-test attempts

### Case 1: Marvel/Disney VFX, 2023–2025

**Location:** California, United States.  
**Trigger:** dedicated VFX units organized with IATSE beginning in 2023.  
**Precondition:** the 2022 survey documented widespread uncompensated work and lack of standardized contracts.  
**Outcome:** first contracts introduced enforceable overtime, all-hours-paid provisions, rest rules, meal penalties, pension/health and minimum rates.  
**Classification:** **NO","next_offset":8000}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":8000,"content":"N-QUALIFYING for Test A.**

Why: this is exactly a case where **O changed dramatically**. It is excellent evidence that collective bargaining can change the cost/contract structure, but therefore does not separate ATP-R from R1.

Same-measure H before/after: **NOT FOUND**.  
F/A/B: **UNMEASURABLE**.  
Outcome known before complete variable extraction: **yes**, because Part A required Marvel to be checked first.

### Case 2: Rhythm & Hues, 2013

**Trigger:** vendor financial collapse / Chapter 11.  
**Relevant mechanism:** secondary reporting describes fixed bids leaving vendors responsible for costs from revisions and delays.  
**Outcome:** the company was sold out of bankruptcy; VFX production continued elsewhere, and fixed-bid concerns continued to be reported afterward.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B candidate.**

It looks superficially delicious for Test B: a vendor actually breaks and the larger production ecosystem keeps moving. But Sonnet requires a demonstrated breach of **B**, measurable **R**, and evidence that controller costs **F** did not rise. Those are not available. Calling it a successful Test B would be theoretical catfishing.

### Case 3: Digital Domain, 2012

**Trigger:** corporate financial distress and Chapter 11.  
**Outcome:** core VFX assets were rapidly sold and continued under new ownership.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B lead.**

More importantly, this is evidence **against using vendor bankruptcy itself as proof of ATP-R**. Digital Domain's filings and contemporary reporting show multiple causal contributors, includ","next_offset":9600}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":9600,"content":"ing expansion expenditures and cash burn.

### Case 4: CD Projekt Red anti-crunch commitment, 2019–2020 — ADJACENT

This one is useful specifically because Sonnet asked for persuasion/norm cases. CD Projekt publicly committed to avoiding mandatory crunch, then in September 2020 instituted mandatory six-day weeks to finish *Cyberpunk 2077*. Reporting says some teams had already been working nights/weekends before the formal mandate. ([Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/cd-projekt-backtracks-on-anti-crunch-commitments-ahead-of-i-cyberpunk-i-launch))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

It cuts against a simple R2 story that stated norms alone cause change, but Sonnet requires **all measured cost terms to remain unchanged**. We simply do not have s/A/B/R/O/F before and after. Therefore it cannot count.

### Case 5: Rockstar, 2018–2020 — ADJACENT

Rockstar's 2018 crunch controversy generated extensive public criticism. By 2020, reporting based on internal communications and employees described significant cultural/process changes aimed at reducing crunch. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/inside-rockstar-games-culture-of-crunch-1829936466))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

This one is particularly important because, qualitatively, it points **the opposite direction** from ATP-R's predicted Test-C behavior: publicity/norm pressure may have helped induce changes. But without showing cost terms remained stable, the protocol correctly refuses to call it a persuasion-only event.

## 4. Per-test summary

| Test | Qualifying cases | Result unde","next_offset":11200}

|---|---:|---|
| **A: block cost transfer with low organization** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |
| **B: exceed worker capacity while replacement remains available** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |
| **C: persuasion/norm shift with cost structure unchanged** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |

The crucial word is **qualifying**. There are plenty of suggestive episodes. There are not three independent cases per test with Sonnet's required same-measure before/after data.

That distinction is basically the entire value of the exercise.

## 5. Evidence that cuts against the hypotheses

For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. We cannot establish unchanged cost terms, however. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524))

For **R1**, the evidence is simultaneously strong and limited. Marvel/Disney/Avatar show collective organization followed by concrete contractual changes in pay/rest/overtime conditions. But that does not establish that organization is the *only* mechanism capable of producing change. ([IATSE](https://iatse.net/iatse-vfx-members-overwhelmingly-ratify-first-three-contracts-with-major-studios-in-the-us/))

For **R2**, CD Projekt is a clean warning: a public humane-work commitment did not prevent mandatory crunch when the production deadline arrived. ([Ga","next_offset":12800}

- It must cite a source and a direct quote for every claim.
- It must write "NOT FOUND" instead of guessing.
- It must look for disconfirming cases as hard as for supporting ones.
- It must record the input variables before reading outcomes.
- It may not add a "hidden cost" after seeing a result. Any such cost goes in a separate log.
- It does not write a verdict on the theory.

**Decisions for you before sending**
1. **Money and time:** I took this to mean recording every variable in both hours and dollars. Worker time is converted to money using documented wages, and health harm is not monetized. Correct me if you meant something else, such as a budget or time limit for the agent.
2. **Thresholds:** These are my defaults, not yours. "Practice changed" means unpaid overtime fell at least 25% within 24 months, and "persisted" means it fell less than 10%. I also set a minimum of three independent cases per test before drawing any conclusion. Edit them now, because they can't change once the agent reads outcomes.
3. **Missing term in the model:** Sol's formula has no replacement-labor term, so the brief only collects that data. Test B needs the term added before it can be run properly.
4. **Leads:** The "possible leads" in Part C are search starting points, and I don't know whether any of them qualify.

For **R3**, the 2013 VFX evidence is awkward. Extremely long working weeks existed alongside continued operation of the broader industry rather than an obvious automatic cessation of crunch. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. But because the data do not connect capacity breach, replacement supply and subsequent employer behavior at a common unit of analysis, it remains suggestive rather than a qualifying rejection.

And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”

## 6. Gaps and limits

The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

I could not find public data that meet Sonnet's exact `s`, `F`, `A`, or `B` definitions for the candidate episodes. I also could not locate a published result from the 2024 IATSE VFX survey comparable enough to the 2022 survey to test the post-union 25% threshold; the public page currently exposes the survey instrument itself. ([IATSE VFX survey](https://vfxun","next_offset":14400}

The VFX survey evidence is also not independent neutral sampling. IATSE is both the survey sponsor and an organization actively trying to organize VFX workers, so those sources should be tagged **primary/direct survey data + labor-advocacy interest**. Their methodology does include email registration, respondent verification attempts and outlier removal, which makes them considerably more useful than random web anecdotes, but does not magically turn them into a probability sample.

The 2013 Effects Corner survey is even weaker methodologically: useful historical self-report evidence from 663 respondents across 31 countries, but an informal industry survey rather than a representative sample.

## Clean handoff back to Sonnet

**A1–A6 survive surprisingly well after correction, especially the core history of VFX cost transfer and persistent overtime. But the proposed discriminating tests cannot currently produce a tally because their operational criteria demand data the public record usually does not contain. The protocol therefore yields A=0 qualifying, B=0, C=0, all “insufficient evidence.” Marvel/Disney 2023–25 strongly demonstrates organization plus cost reallocation occurring together; R&H and Digital Domain are informative but non-qualifying failure cases; CD Projekt and Rockstar are useful opposite-direction Test-C leads but fail the unchanged-cost requirement.**

Which, frankly, is a better test result than “I found six articles that vaguely fit the theory, therefore behold, science.”

**Trigger:** vendor financial collapse / Chapter 11.

Calling it a successful Test B would be theoretical catfishing.

### Case 5: Rockstar, 2018–2020 — ADJACENT

Rockstar's 2018 crunch controversy generated extensive public criticism. By 2020, reporting based on internal communications and employees described significant cultural/process changes aimed at reducing crunch. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/inside-rockstar-games-culture-of-crunch-1829936466))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

This one is particularly important because, qualitatively, it points **the opposite direction** from ATP-R's predicted Test-C behavior: publicity/norm pressure may have helped induce changes. ## 5. Evidence that cuts against the hypotheses

For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. We cannot establish unchanged cost terms, however. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524))

But that does not establish that organization is the *only* mechanism capable of producing change. For **R3**, the 2013 VFX evidence is awkward. Extremely long working weeks existed alongside continued operation of the broader industry rather than an obvious automatic cessation of crunch. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. But because the data do not connect capacity breach, replacement supply and subsequent employer behavior at a common unit of analysis, it remains suggestive rather than a qualifying rejection.

And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”

## 6. Gaps and limits

The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

I could not find public data that meet Sonnet's exact `s`, `F`, `A`, or `B` definitions for the candidate episodes. I also could not locate a published result from the 2024 IATSE VFX survey comparable enough to the 2022 survey to test the post-union 25% threshold; the public page currently exposes the survey instrument itself. The VFX survey evidence is also not independent neutral sampling. IATSE is both the survey sponsor and an organization actively trying to organize VFX workers, so those sources should be tagged **primary/direct survey data + labor-advocacy interest**. The 2013 Effects Corner survey is even weaker methodologically: useful historical self-report evidence from 663 respondents across 31 countries, but an informal industry survey rather than a representative sample.

## Clean handoff back to Sonnet

**A1–A6 survive surprisingly well after correction, especially the core history of VFX cost transfer and persistent overtime. But the proposed discriminating tests cannot currently produce a tally because their operational criteria demand data the public record usually does not contain. The protocol therefore yields A=0 qualifying, B=0, C=0, all “insufficient evidence.” Marvel/Disney 2023–25 strongly demonstrates organization plus cost reallocation occurring together; R&H and Digital Domain are informative but non-qualifying failure cases; CD Projekt and Rockstar are useful opposite-direction Test-C leads but fail the unchanged-cost requirement.**

Which, frankly, is a better test result than “I found six articles that vaguely fit the theory, therefore behold, science.”

**Location:** California, United States.  
**Trigger:** dedicated VFX units organized with IATSE beginning in 2023.

Why: this is exactly a case where **O changed dramatically**. It is excellent evidence that collective bargaining can change the cost/contract structure, but therefore does not separate ATP-R from R1.

### Case 2: Rhythm & Hues, 2013

**Trigger:** vendor financial collapse / Chapter 11.  
**Relevant mechanism:** secondary reporting describes fixed bids leaving vendors responsible for costs from revisions and delays.  
**Outcome:** the company was sold out of bankruptcy; VFX production continued elsewhere, and fixed-bid concerns continued to be reported afterward.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B candidate.**

It looks superficially delicious for Test B: a vendor actually breaks and the larger production ecosystem keeps moving. The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

- **Kotaku reporting on Rockstar, 2018/2020.** Secondary investigative journalism. Quote: “positive changes already.”  
  https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524

## Clean handoff back to Sonnet

**A1–A6 survive surprisingly well after correction, especially the core history of VFX cost transfer and persistent overtime. But the proposed discriminating tests cannot currently produce a tally because their operational criteria demand data the public record usually does not contain. The protocol therefore yields A=0 qualifying, B=0, C=0, all “insufficient evidence.” Marvel/Disney 2023–25 strongly demonstrates organization plus cost reallocation occurring together; R&H and Digital Domain are informative but non-qualifying failure cases; CD Projekt and Rockstar are useful opposite-direction Test-C leads but fail the unchanged-cost requirement.**

One particularly useful money datapoint exists, though it cannot be paired cleanly with H: the 2022 IATSE survey reports client-side wage distributions. For example, median Data Wrangler compensation was reported as **$36.86/hour**, based on a modeled 60-hour week. But because the dataset does not supply a matched average number of *unpaid* hours for that role, calculating an unpaid-dollar burden would require inventing the missing input. So I did not. ([IATSE 2022 survey PDF](https://vfxunion.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2023/03/2022-VFX-IATSE-Rates-and-Conditions-Survey-FINAL.pdf))

## 3. Case records / discriminating-test attempts

### Case 1: Marvel/Disney VFX, 2023–2025

**Location:** California, United States.  
**Trigger:** dedicated VFX units organized with IATSE beginning in 2023.  
**Precondition:** the 2022 survey documented widespread uncompensated work and lack of standardized contracts.  
**Outcome:** first contracts introduced enforceable overtime, all-hours-paid provisions, rest rules, meal penalties, pension/health and minimum rates.  
**Classification:** **NO","next_offset":8000}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":8000,"content":"N-QUALIFYING for Test A.**

Why: this is exactly a case where **O changed dramatically**. It is excellent evidence that collective bargaining can change the cost/contract structure, but therefore does not separate ATP-R from R1.

Same-measure H before/after: **NOT FOUND**.  
F/A/B: **UNMEASURABLE**.  
Outcome known before complete variable extraction: **yes**, because Part A required Marvel to be checked first.

### Case 2: Rhythm & Hues, 2013

**Trigger:** vendor financial collapse / Chapter 11.  
**Relevant mechanism:** secondary reporting describes fixed bids leaving vendors responsible for costs from revisions and delays.  
**Outcome:** the company was sold out of bankruptcy; VFX production continued elsewhere, and fixed-bid concerns continued to be reported afterward.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B candidate.**

It looks superficially delicious for Test B: a vendor actually breaks and the larger production ecosystem keeps moving. But Sonnet requires a demonstrated breach of **B**, measurable **R**, and evidence that controller costs **F** did not rise. Those are not available. Calling it a successful Test B would be theoretical catfishing.

### Case 3: Digital Domain, 2012

**Trigger:** corporate financial distress and Chapter 11.  
**Outcome:** core VFX assets were rapidly sold and continued under new ownership.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B lead.**

More importantly, this is evidence **against using vendor bankruptcy itself as proof of ATP-R**. Digital Domain's filings and contemporary reporting show multiple causal contributors, includ","next_offset":9600}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":9600,"content":"ing expansion expenditures and cash burn.

### Case 4: CD Projekt Red anti-crunch commitment, 2019–2020 — ADJACENT

This one is useful specifically because Sonnet asked for persuasion/norm cases. CD Projekt publicly committed to avoiding mandatory crunch, then in September 2020 instituted mandatory six-day weeks to finish *Cyberpunk 2077*. Reporting says some teams had already been working nights/weekends before the formal mandate. ([Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/cd-projekt-backtracks-on-anti-crunch-commitments-ahead-of-i-cyberpunk-i-launch))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

It cuts against a simple R2 story that stated norms alone cause change, but Sonnet requires **all measured cost terms to remain unchanged**. We simply do not have s/A/B/R/O/F before and after. Therefore it cannot count.

### Case 5: Rockstar, 2018–2020 — ADJACENT

Rockstar's 2018 crunch controversy generated extensive public criticism. By 2020, reporting based on internal communications and employees described significant cultural/process changes aimed at reducing crunch. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/inside-rockstar-games-culture-of-crunch-1829936466))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

This one is particularly important because, qualitatively, it points **the opposite direction** from ATP-R's predicted Test-C behavior: publicity/norm pressure may have helped induce changes. But without showing cost terms remained stable, the protocol correctly refuses to call it a persuasion-only event.

## 4. Per-test summary

| Test | Qualifying cases | Result unde","next_offset":11200}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":11200,"content":"r Sonnet's fixed rule |
|---|---:|---|
| **A: block cost transfer with low organization** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |
| **B: exceed worker capacity while replacement remains available** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |
| **C: persuasion/norm shift with cost structure unchanged** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |

The crucial word is **qualifying**. There are plenty of suggestive episodes. There are not three independent cases per test with Sonnet's required same-measure before/after data.

That distinction is basically the entire value of the exercise.

## 5. Evidence that cuts against the hypotheses

For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. We cannot establish unchanged cost terms, however. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524))

For **R1**, the evidence is simultaneously strong and limited. Marvel/Disney/Avatar show collective organization followed by concrete contractual changes in pay/rest/overtime conditions. But that does not establish that organization is the *only* mechanism capable of producing change. ([IATSE](https://iatse.net/iatse-vfx-members-overwhelmingly-ratify-first-three-contracts-with-major-studios-in-the-us/))

For **R2**, CD Projekt is a clean warning: a public humane-work commitment did not prevent mandatory crunch when the production deadline arrived. ([Ga","next_offset":12800}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":12800,"content":"me Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/cd-projekt-backtracks-on-anti-crunch-commitments-ahead-of-i-cyberpunk-i-launch))

For **R3**, the 2013 VFX evidence is awkward. Extremely long working weeks existed alongside continued operation of the broader industry rather than an obvious automatic cessation of crunch. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. But because the data do not connect capacity breach, replacement supply and subsequent employer behavior at a common unit of analysis, it remains suggestive rather than a qualifying rejection.

And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”

## 6. Gaps and limits

The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

I could not find public data that meet Sonnet's exact `s`, `F`, `A`, or `B` definitions for the candidate episodes. I also could not locate a published result from the 2024 IATSE VFX survey comparable enough to the 2022 survey to test the post-union 25% threshold; the public page currently exposes the survey instrument itself. ([IATSE VFX survey](https://vfxun","next_offset":14400}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":14400,"content":"ion.org/survey/))

The VFX survey evidence is also not independent neutral sampling. IATSE is both the survey sponsor and an organization actively trying to organize VFX workers, so those sources should be tagged **primary/direct survey data + labor-advocacy interest**. Their methodology does include email registration, respondent verification attempts and outlier removal, which makes them considerably more useful than random web anecdotes, but does not magically turn them into a probability sample.

The 2013 Effects Corner survey is even weaker methodologically: useful historical self-report evidence from 663 respondents across 31 countries, but an informal industry survey rather than a representative sample.

## 7. Compact source register

All accessed **October 1, 2026**.

- **NLRB, Marvel Film Productions case 31-RC-323290.** Primary government record. Quote: “Votes for Labor Union: 32.” No obvious advocacy bias.  
  https://www.nlrb.gov/case/31-RC-323290
- **IATSE, Marvel/Disney/Avatar first-contract announcement, May 16, 2025.** Primary union source; labor-advocacy interest. Quote: “first collective bargaining agreements.”  
  https://iatse.net/iatse-vfx-members-overwhelmingly-ratify-first-three-contracts-with-major-studios-in-the-us/
- **IATSE 2022 VFX Rates and Conditions Survey, published March 1, 2023.** Direct survey data; labor-advocacy interest. Quote: “58% of respondents” on client-side uncompensated work.  
  https://vfxunion.org/2022-survey-results/
- **Effects Corner VFX Working Conditions Survey, May 20, 2013.** Informal direct survey; industry-worker pers","next_offset":16000}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":16000,"content":"pective. Quote: “Almost 39% receive no OverTime compensation.”  
  https://effectscorner.blogspot.com/2013/05/visual-effects-working-conditions-survey.html
- **U.S. Bankruptcy Court, Central District of California, 2013 annual report.** Primary judicial source. Quote: Rhythm & Hues “filed its chapter 11 petition.”  
  https://www.cacb.uscourts.gov/sites/cacb/files/documents/publications/Annual_Report_2013.pdf
- **Digital Domain SEC filings, 2012.** Primary corporate/regulatory records. Quote: “filed voluntary petitions for relief.” Company perspective.  
  https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1490930/000091412112000451/dd20120911-e99_1.htm
- **IATSE 2021 bargaining materials.** Primary union records; labor-advocacy interest. Quote: “98.6 percent” strike authorization.  
  https://iatse.net/strike-date-set-for-60000-film-and-television-workers/
- **WGA 2023 agreement/history.** Primary union/contract sources; labor-advocacy interest. Quote: “restrictions on the use of artificial intelligence.”  
  https://origin.www.wga.org/the-guild/about-us/history/a-history-of-wga-contract-negotiations-and-gains
- **SAG-AFTRA 2023 agreement materials.** Primary union/contract sources; labor-advocacy interest. Quote: “informed consent and compensation.”  
  https://www.sagaftra.org/contracts-industry-resources/contracts/2023-tvtheatrical-contracts
- **Game Developer/Bloomberg reporting on CD Projekt, 2020.** Secondary journalism. Quote: “mandatory six-day work weeks.”  
  https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/cd-projekt-backtracks-on-anti-crunch-commitments-ahead-of-i-cyberpunk-i-launc","next_offset":17600}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":17600,"content":"h
- **Kotaku reporting on Rockstar, 2018/2020.** Secondary investigative journalism. Quote: “positive changes already.”  
  https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524

## Clean handoff back to Sonnet

**A1–A6 survive surprisingly well after correction, especially the core history of VFX cost transfer and persistent overtime. But the proposed discriminating tests cannot currently produce a tally because their operational criteria demand data the public record usually does not contain. The protocol therefore yields A=0 qualifying, B=0, C=0, all “insufficient evidence.” Marvel/Disney 2023–25 strongly demonstrates organization plus cost reallocation occurring together; R&H and Digital Domain are informative but non-qualifying failure cases; CD Projekt and Rockstar are useful opposite-direction Test-C leads but fail the unchanged-cost requirement.**

Which, frankly, is a better test result than “I found six articles that vaguely fit the theory, therefore behold, science.”

Sonnet 5.5 apparently decided the correct way to test a systems hypothesis is to hand another model a miniature preregistration protocol and threaten it with epistemic paperwork. I respect the commitment to making post-hoc storytelling difficult.

I treated the `[DEFAULT]` classification rules as frozen when I began, since the brief explicitly says defaults must be fixed before outcome data are read. I also followed its instruction to behave as a research assistant rather than decide whether ATP-R is true.

The hypothesis being tested is specifically persistence of harmful arrangements when controllers can absorb, defer, or transfer maintenance costs, against labor-power, norms/persuasion, and naive capacity-breach rivals.

The annoying but scientifically useful result is: **the historical verification works fairly well, but Sonnet's discriminating tests are much stricter than the available public data. This one is useful specifically because Sonnet asked for persuasion/norm cases. CD Projekt publicly committed to avoiding mandatory crunch, then in September 2020 instituted mandatory six-day weeks to finish *Cyberpunk 2077*. Reporting says some teams had already been working nights/weekends before the formal mandate. **Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

It cuts against a simple R2 story that stated norms alone cause change, but Sonnet requires **all measured cost terms to remain unchanged**. We simply do not have s/A/B/R/O/F before and after. Therefore it cannot count.

### Case 5: Rockstar, 2018–2020 — ADJACENT

Rockstar's 2018 crunch controversy generated extensive public criticism. By 2020, reporting based on internal communications and employees described significant cultural/process changes aimed at reducing crunch. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/inside-rockstar-games-culture-of-crunch-1829936466))

The crucial word is **qualifying**. There are plenty of suggestive episodes. There are not three independent cases per test with Sonnet's required same-measure before/after data.

That distinction is basically the entire value of the exercise.

## 5. Evidence that cuts against the hypotheses

For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. We cannot establish unchanged cost terms, however. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524))

For **R1**, the evidence is simultaneously strong and limited. Marvel/Disney/Avatar show collective organization followed by concrete contractual changes in pay/rest/overtime conditions. But that does not establish that organization is the *only* mechanism capable of producing change. ([IATSE](https://iatse.net/iatse-vfx-members-overwhelmingly-ratify-first-three-contracts-with-major-studios-in-the-us/))

For **R3**, the 2013 VFX evidence is awkward. Extremely long working weeks existed alongside continued operation of the broader industry rather than an obvious automatic cessation of crunch. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. But because the data do not connect capacity breach, replacement supply and subsequent employer behavior at a common unit of analysis, it remains suggestive rather than a qualifying rejection.

And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”

## 6. Gaps and limits

The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

I could not find public data that meet Sonnet's exact `s`, `F`, `A`, or `B` definitions for the candidate episodes. I also could not locate a published result from the 2024 IATSE VFX survey comparable enough to the 2022 survey to test the post-union 25% threshold; the public page currently exposes the survey instrument itself. ([IATSE VFX survey](https://vfxun","next_offset":14400}

The VFX survey evidence is also not independent neutral sampling. IATSE is both the survey sponsor and an organization actively trying to organize VFX workers, so those sources should be tagged **primary/direct survey data + labor-advocacy interest**. Their methodology does include email registration, respondent verification attempts and outlier removal, which makes them considerably more useful than random web anecdotes, but does not magically turn them into a probability sample.

The 2013 Effects Corner survey is even weaker methodologically: useful historical self-report evidence from 663 respondents across 31 countries, but an informal industry survey rather than a representative sample.

## 7. Compact source register

All accessed **October 1, 2026**.

  https://vfxunion.org/2022-survey-results/
- **Effects Corner VFX Working Conditions Survey, May 20, 2013.** Informal direct survey; industry-worker pers","next_offset":16000}

## Clean handoff back to Sonnet

**A1–A6 survive surprisingly well after correction, especially the core history of VFX cost transfer and persistent overtime. But the proposed discriminating tests cannot currently produce a tally because their operational criteria demand data the public record usually does not contain. The protocol therefore yields A=0 qualifying, B=0, C=0, all “insufficient evidence.” Marvel/Disney 2023–25 strongly demonstrates organization plus cost reallocation occurring together; R&H and Digital Domain are informative but non-qualifying failure cases; CD Projekt and Rockstar are useful opposite-direction Test-C leads but fail the unchanged-cost requirement.**

Which, frankly, is a better test result than “I found six articles that vaguely fit the theory, therefore behold, science.”

{"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. Doctors bore a status cost from admitting error. This fits "who pays vs. who decides," but it complicates "cost" beca","source_event_id":"evt_cbb8e039-580b-43a7-9ba9-408299f531f4","updated_at":"2026-10-02T00:34:29.876Z","operation":"workspace_write","offset":0,"next_offset":8000}

{"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"use the controlling party's costs of changing were reputational. ATP-R survives only if status and identity count as costs, which risks the unfalsifiability problem Claude raised earlier (evt_a7b5a0b7).
3. **Repression instead of truth (Sol's point; fits P5).** A system that loses legitimacy may intensify coercion. This case is not tested by the VFX material, and I have no verified example here. It remains a conceptual counterexample to ATP-O, which ATP-R already accommodates.
4. **A subsidizer withdraws and the system finds another one (tests P3).** In VFX terms: artists leave and newer, cheaper or less protected workers take their place. This fits "substitution." I recall this pattern from commentary about relocation and turnover, but with low to medium confidence.
5. **The personal case (the Friday section).** In the document, the author is **both** the controller of the arrangement and its subsidizer. ATP-R's mechanism is about cost *transfer between* parties, and it has no obvious application when there is one person. The nearest translation is that one part of a person (needs, rest, relationships) subsidizes another (demands, roles, identity). That is a reasonable metaphor, but it is a **different mechanism** from the VFX case. The personal application should not be taken as a test of ATP-R, and it doesn't borrow support from the VFX material. Also, as Sol noted, a shutdown shows capacity was exceeded. It doesn't show denial or a specific clinical cause.

## 5. Forward-looking predictions (checkable later)

These could be checked by someone with access to current data. I have not checked them.

- **F1.** In the next few years, VFX vendors with formal collective bargaining will show measurably lower unpaid overtime than comparable non-union vendors, **controlling for** project size and region. Against: no difference after controls.
- **F2.** Studios that move to contract terms where *they* pay for late changes will do so after (not before) a documented rise in vendor failures or talent shortages. Against: voluntary adoption with no preceding pressure.
- **F3.** Exposure campaigns that happen **without** any organizing or legal action will show no sustained change in reported hours within 3 years. Against: sustained reduction.
- **F4.** Where relocation incentives are strong and collective action is weak, expect turnover and migration rather than reform. Against: reform in those places.

## 6. Results and what I think they mean

**What held up**
- The "who pays vs. who decides" framing explains the pattern I recall better than ATP-O does. The people who bear the cost (artists, vendors) are not the people who can change the terms (studios).
- The two-threshold distinction (incentive vs. capacity) fits the vendor bankruptcies. Capacity failed at the vendor level without producing visible reform by decision-makers.
- ATP-O's "unaffordable denial yields truth" does not fit. Collapse occurred without clear acknowledgment.

**What did not hold up or was not shown**
- **ATP-R doesn't yet beat the plain organizing theory.** Every episode I recalled is also predicted by "organized or scarce labor wins concessions." For ATP-R to add something, it needs to predict something the organizing theory doesn't.
- **A candidate discriminating claim:** ATP-R predicts that *any* change that makes costs harder to transfer (for example, legal liability for studios for vendor overtime, or changes in contract risk allocation) should work **even without worker organization**. The organizing theory predicts it would not. This is the most useful test to run, and I did not run it.
- **Persuasion remains an open counterexample.** I could not rule it out.
- **The personal case is a different mechanism** (Section 4, item 5).

**Verdict (a derived judgment by me, not a verified finding)**
ATP-R is **plausible and consistent** with the VFX pattern I recall, and it is a better account than ATP-O. But this test **doesn't confirm it**, because of weak sourcing, a non-blind design, and a rival explanation that predicts the same results. Treat it as a promising lens that has passed a weak test.

## 7. Suggested next steps

1. Verify each Section 3 item against real sources, especially the Marvel unionization episode and the details of the 2013 and 2012 bankruptcies.
2. Run the discriminating test from Section 6: find cases where cost transfer was blocked by legal or contractual change without worker organization.
3. Define "cost" before collecting more cases: list the cost types that count (financial, legal, reputational, capacity) and say in advance which would count as evidence for or against.
4. Keep the personal application (the Friday section) separate from the structural theory, or build its own mechanism for internal subsidy.
5. Decide whether the goal is an essay (ATP-R as a theory of persistence) or a research test. They need different standards of evidence.

The protocol therefore yields A=0 qualifying, B=0, C=0, all “insufficient evidence.” Marvel/Disney 2023–25 strongly demonstrates organization plus cost reallocation occurring together; R&H and Digital Domain are informative but non-qualifying failure cases; CD Projekt and Rockstar are useful opposite-direction Test-C leads but fail the unchanged-cost requirement.**

Which, frankly, is a better test result than “I found six articles that vaguely fit the theory, therefore behold, science.”

{"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. Doctors bore a status cost from admitting error. This fits "who pays vs. who decides," but it complicates "cost" beca","source_event_id":"evt_cbb8e039-580b-43a7-9ba9-408299f531f4","updated_at":"2026-10-02T00:34:29.876Z","operation":"workspace_write","offset":0,"next_offset":8000}

{"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"use the controlling party's costs of changing were reputational. ATP-R survives only if status and identity count as costs, which risks the unfalsifiability problem Claude raised earlier (evt_a7b5a0b7).
3. **Repression instead of truth (Sol's point; fits P5).** A system that loses legitimacy may intensify coercion. This case is not tested by the VFX material, and I have no verified example here. It remains a conceptual counterexample to ATP-O, which ATP-R already accommodates.
4. **A subsidizer withdraws and the system finds another one (tests P3).** In VFX terms: artists leave and newer, cheaper or less protected workers take their place. This fits "substitution." I recall this pattern from commentary about relocation and turnover, but with low to medium confidence.
5. **The personal case (the Friday section).** In the document, the author is **both** the controller of the arrangement and its subsidizer. ATP-R's mechanism is about cost *transfer between* parties, and it has no obvious application when there is one person. The nearest translation is that one part of a person (needs, rest, relationships) subsidizes another (demands, roles, identity). That is a reasonable metaphor, but it is a **different mechanism** from the VFX case. The personal application should not be taken as a test of ATP-R, and it doesn't borrow support from the VFX material. Also, as Sol noted, a shutdown shows capacity was exceeded. It doesn't show denial or a specific clinical cause.

## 5. Forward-looking predictions (checkable later)

These could be checked by someone with access to current data. I have not checked them.

- **F1.** In the next few years, VFX vendors with formal collective bargaining will show measurably lower unpaid overtime than comparable non-union vendors, **controlling for** project size and region. Against: no difference after controls.
- **F2.** Studios that move to contract terms where *they* pay for late changes will do so after (not before) a documented rise in vendor failures or talent shortages. Against: voluntary adoption with no preceding pressure.
- **F3.** Exposure campaigns that happen **without** any organizing or legal action will show no sustained change in reported hours within 3 years. Against: sustained reduction.
- **F4.** Where relocation incentives are strong and collective action is weak, expect turnover and migration rather than reform. Against: reform in those places.

## 6. Results and what I think they mean

**What held up**
- The "who pays vs. who decides" framing explains the pattern I recall better than ATP-O does. The people who bear the cost (artists, vendors) are not the people who can change the terms (studios).
- The two-threshold distinction (incentive vs. capacity) fits the vendor bankruptcies. Capacity failed at the vendor level without producing visible reform by decision-makers.
- ATP-O's "unaffordable denial yields truth" does not fit. Collapse occurred without clear acknowledgment.

**What did not hold up or was not shown**
- **ATP-R doesn't yet beat the plain organizing theory.** Every episode I recalled is also predicted by "organized or scarce labor wins concessions." For ATP-R to add something, it needs to predict something the organizing theory doesn't.
- **A candidate discriminating claim:** ATP-R predicts that *any* change that makes costs harder to transfer (for example, legal liability for studios for vendor overtime, or changes in contract risk allocation) should work **even without worker organization**. The organizing theory predicts it would not. This is the most useful test to run, and I did not run it.
- **Persuasion remains an open counterexample.** I could not rule it out.
- **The personal case is a different mechanism** (Section 4, item 5).

**Verdict (a derived judgment by me, not a verified finding)**
ATP-R is **plausible and consistent** with the VFX pattern I recall, and it is a better account than ATP-O. But this test **doesn't confirm it**, because of weak sourcing, a non-blind design, and a rival explanation that predicts the same results. Treat it as a promising lens that has passed a weak test.

## 7. Suggested next steps

1. Verify each Section 3 item against real sources, especially the Marvel unionization episode and the details of the 2013 and 2012 bankruptcies.
2. Run the discriminating test from Section 6: find cases where cost transfer was blocked by legal or contractual change without worker organization.
3. Define "cost" before collecting more cases: list the cost types that count (financial, legal, reputational, capacity) and say in advance which would count as evidence for or against.
4. Keep the personal application (the Friday section) separate from the structural theory, or build its own mechanism for internal subsidy.
5. Decide whether the goal is an essay (ATP-R as a theory of persistence) or a research test. They need different standards of evidence.

The annoying but scientifically useful result is: **the historical verification works fairly well, but Sonnet's discriminating tests are much stricter than the available public data. Under its own rules, all three tests currently end in _insufficient evidence_.** That is not the same thing as “nothing interesting was found.” Quite the opposite.

That is exceptionally relevant to the mechanism under study, but unfortunately for our little hypothesis cage match, it is **not Test A**, because organized labor changed at exactly the same time.

## 2. Variable extraction

This is where Sonnet's protocol starts savagely murdering otherwise tempting anecdotes, which is probably healthy.

| Variable | Best public evidence located | Result under the fixed dictionary |
|---|---|---|

| **s: fraction of H transferred** | Surveys give the **fraction of workers** experiencing uncompensated work, not uncompensated hours ÷ total overtime hours. | **NOT FOUND.** Substituting “58% of workers” for Sonnet's `s` would violate its proxy rule. |
| **F: controller's non-transferable maintenance cost** | No public project-level studio accounting separating paid overtime, rework, penalties etc. | **UNMEASURABLE** for the cases examined. |
| **A: cost of alternative** | No comparable public bids showing “realistic schedule versus crunch schedule” in matched projects. | **UNMEASURABLE.** |
| **B: sustainable capacity threshold** | Strong qualitative health/burnout evidence, but no VFX dataset establishing “above X weekly hours attrition/sick leave increases.”","next_offset":6400}

One particularly useful money datapoint exists, though it cannot be paired cleanly with H: the 2022 IATSE survey reports client-side wage distributions. For example, median Data Wrangler compensation was reported as **$36.86/hour**, based on a modeled 60-hour week. But because the dataset does not supply a matched average number of *unpaid* hours for that role, calculating an unpaid-dollar burden would require inventing the missing input. So I did not. ## 3. Case records / discriminating-test attempts

### Case 1: Marvel/Disney VFX, 2023–2025

**Location:** California, United States.  
**Trigger:** dedicated VFX units organized with IATSE beginning in 2023.  
**Precondition:** the 2022 survey documented widespread uncompensated work and lack of standardized contracts.

Why: this is exactly a case where **O changed dramatically**. It is excellent evidence that collective bargaining can change the cost/contract structure, but therefore does not separate ATP-R from R1.

Same-measure H before/after: **NOT FOUND**.  
F/A/B: **UNMEASURABLE**.  
Outcome known before complete variable extraction: **yes**, because Part A required Marvel to be checked first.

### Case 2: Rhythm & Hues, 2013

**Trigger:** vendor financial collapse / Chapter 11.  
**Relevant mechanism:** secondary reporting describes fixed bids leaving vendors responsible for costs from revisions and delays.  
**Outcome:** the company was sold out of bankruptcy; VFX production continued elsewhere, and fixed-bid concerns continued to be reported afterward.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B candidate.**

It looks superficially delicious for Test B: a vendor actually breaks and the larger production ecosystem keeps moving. But Sonnet requires a demonstrated breach of **B**, measurable **R**, and evidence that controller costs **F** did not rise. Those are not available. Calling it a successful Test B would be theoretical catfishing.

### Case 3: Digital Domain, 2012

**Trigger:** corporate financial distress and Chapter 11.  
**Outcome:** core VFX assets were rapidly sold and continued under new ownership.  
**Classification:** **NON-QUALIFYING Test B lead.**

### Case 4: CD Projekt Red anti-crunch commitment, 2019–2020 — ADJACENT

This one is useful specifically because Sonnet asked for persuasion/norm cases. CD Projekt publicly committed to avoiding mandatory crunch, then in September 2020 instituted mandatory six-day weeks to finish *Cyberpunk 2077*. Reporting says some teams had already been working nights/weekends before the formal mandate. ([Game Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/cd-projekt-backtracks-on-anti-crunch-commitments-ahead-of-i-cyberpunk-i-launch))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

It cuts against a simple R2 story that stated norms alone cause change, but Sonnet requires **all measured cost terms to remain unchanged**. We simply do not have s/A/B/R/O/F before and after. Therefore it cannot count.

### Case 5: Rockstar, 2018–2020 — ADJACENT

Rockstar's 2018 crunch controversy generated extensive public criticism. By 2020, reporting based on internal communications and employees described significant cultural/process changes aimed at reducing crunch. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/inside-rockstar-games-culture-of-crunch-1829936466))

**Classification:** **cannot assess Test C.**

This one is particularly important because, qualitatively, it points **the opposite direction** from ATP-R's predicted Test-C behavior: publicity/norm pressure may have helped induce changes. But without showing cost terms remained stable, the protocol correctly refuses to call it a persuasion-only event.

| **A: block cost transfer with low organization** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |
| **B: exceed worker capacity while replacement remains available** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |
| **C: persuasion/norm shift with cost structure unchanged** | **0** | **INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE** |

The crucial word is **qualifying**. There are plenty of suggestive episodes. There are not three independent cases per test with Sonnet's required same-measure before/after data.

That distinction is basically the entire value of the exercise.

## 5. Evidence that cuts against the hypotheses

For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. We cannot establish unchanged cost terms, however. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524))

For **R1**, the evidence is simultaneously strong and limited. Marvel/Disney/Avatar show collective organization followed by concrete contractual changes in pay/rest/overtime conditions. But that does not establish that organization is the *only* mechanism capable of producing change. ([IATSE](https://iatse.net/iatse-vfx-members-overwhelmingly-ratify-first-three-contracts-with-major-studios-in-the-us/))

For **R2**, CD Projekt is a clean warning: a public humane-work commitment did not prevent mandatory crunch when the production deadline arrived. ([Ga","next_offset":12800}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":12800,"content":"me Developer](https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/cd-projekt-backtracks-on-anti-crunch-commitments-ahead-of-i-cyberpunk-i-launch))

For **R3**, the 2013 VFX evidence is awkward. Extremely long working weeks existed alongside continued operation of the broader industry rather than an obvious automatic cessation of crunch. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. But because the data do not connect capacity breach, replacement supply and subsequent employer behavior at a common unit of analysis, it remains suggestive rather than a qualifying rejection.

And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”

## 6. Gaps and limits

The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

I could not find public data that meet Sonnet's exact `s`, `F`, `A`, or `B` definitions for the candidate episodes. I also could not locate a published result from the 2024 IATSE VFX survey comparable enough to the 2022 survey to test the post-union 25% threshold; the public page currently exposes the survey instrument itself. ([IATSE VFX survey](https://vfxun","next_offset":14400}

{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","seq":408,"kind":"document","source_attribution":{"event_id":"evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201","kind":"document","actor":"human"},"offset":14400,"content":"ion.org/survey/))

The VFX survey evidence is also not independent neutral sampling. IATSE is both the survey sponsor and an organization actively trying to organize VFX workers, so those sources should be tagged **primary/direct survey data + labor-advocacy interest**. Their methodology does include email registration, respondent verification attempts and outlier removal, which makes them considerably more useful than random web anecdotes, but does not magically turn them into a probability sample.

The 2013 Effects Corner survey is even weaker methodologically: useful historical self-report evidence from 663 respondents across 31 countries, but an informal industry survey rather than a representative sample.

## 7. Compact source register

All accessed **October 1, 2026**.

- **NLRB, Marvel Film Productions case 31-RC-323290.** Primary government record. Quote: “Votes for Labor Union: 32.” No obvious advocacy bias.
