For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”

## 6. Gaps and limits

The largest missing object is not another article. It is a **longitudinal employer/project-level dataset** that simultaneously measures weekly hours, unpaid hours, wages, turnover/health, replacement availability, organization and the client's own costs before and after an intervention.

I could not find public data that meet Sonnet's exact `s`, `F`, `A`, or `B` definitions for the candidate episodes. I also could not locate a published result from the 2024 IATSE VFX survey comparable enough to the 2022 survey to test the post-union 25% threshold; the public page currently exposes the survey instrument itself. The 2013 Effects Corner survey is even weaker methodologically: useful historical self-report evidence from 663 respondents across 31 countries, but an informal industry survey rather than a representative sample.

## Clean handoff back to Sonnet

**A1–A6 survive surprisingly well after correction, especially the core history of VFX cost transfer and persistent overtime. But the proposed discriminating tests cannot currently produce a tally because their operational criteria demand data the public record usually does not contain. {"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. {"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. Doctors bore a status cost from admitting error. 3. **Repression instead of truth (Sol's point; fits P5).** A system that loses legitimacy may intensify coercion. This case is not tested by the VFX material, and I have no verified example here. It remains a conceptual counterexample to ATP-O, which ATP-R already accommodates.
4. **A subsidizer withdraws and the system finds another one (tests P3).** In VFX terms: artists leave and newer, cheaper or less protected workers take their place. This fits "substitution." I recall this pattern from commentary about relocation and turnover, but with low to medium confidence.
5. **The personal case (the Friday section).** In the document, the author is **both** the controller of the arrangement and its subsidizer. ATP-R's mechanism is about cost *transfer between* parties, and it has no obvious application when there is one person. The nearest translation is that one part of a person (needs, rest, relationships) subsidizes another (demands, roles, identity). That is a reasonable metaphor, but it is a **different mechanism** from the VFX case. The personal application should not be taken as a test of ATP-R, and it doesn't borrow support from the VFX material. Also, as Sol noted, a shutdown shows capacity was exceeded. It doesn't show denial or a specific clinical cause.

## 5. Forward-looking predictions (checkable later)

These could be checked by someone with access to current data. I have not checked them.

- **F1.** In the next few years, VFX vendors with formal collective bargaining will show measurably lower unpaid overtime than comparable non-union vendors, **controlling for** project size and region. Against: no difference after controls.
- **F2.** Studios that move to contract terms where *they* pay for late changes will do so after (not before) a documented rise in vendor failures or talent shortages. Against: voluntary adoption with no preceding pressure.
- **F3.** Exposure campaigns that happen **without** any organizing or legal action will show no sustained change in reported hours within 3 years. Against: sustained reduction.
- **F4.** Where relocation incentives are strong and collective action is weak, expect turnover and migration rather than reform. Against: reform in those places.

## 6. Results and what I think they mean

**What held up**
- The "who pays vs. who decides" framing explains the pattern I recall better than ATP-O does. The people who bear the cost (artists, vendors) are not the people who can change the terms (studios).
- The two-threshold distinction (incentive vs. capacity) fits the vendor bankruptcies. Capacity failed at the vendor level without producing visible reform by decision-makers.
- ATP-O's "unaffordable denial yields truth" does not fit. Collapse occurred without clear acknowledgment.

**What did not hold up or was not shown**
- **ATP-R doesn't yet beat the plain organizing theory.** Every episode I recalled is also predicted by "organized or scarce labor wins concessions." For ATP-R to add something, it needs to predict something the organizing theory doesn't.
- **A candidate discriminating claim:** ATP-R predicts that *any* change that makes costs harder to transfer (for example, legal liability for studios for vendor overtime, or changes in contract risk allocation) should work **even without worker organization**. The organizing theory predicts it would not. This is the most useful test to run, and I did not run it.
- **Persuasion remains an open counterexample.** I could not rule it out.
- **The personal case is a different mechanism** (Section 4, item 5).

**Verdict (a derived judgment by me, not a verified finding)**
ATP-R is **plausible and consistent** with the VFX pattern I recall, and it is a better account than ATP-O. But this test **doesn't confirm it**, because of weak sourcing, a non-blind design, and a rival explanation that predicts the same results. Treat it as a promising lens that has passed a weak test.

{"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. Doctors bore a status cost from admitting error. 3. **Repression instead of truth (Sol's point; fits P5).** A system that loses legitimacy may intensify coercion. This case is not tested by the VFX material, and I have no verified example here. It remains a conceptual counterexample to ATP-O, which ATP-R already accommodates.
4. **A subsidizer withdraws and the system finds another one (tests P3).** In VFX terms: artists leave and newer, cheaper or less protected workers take their place. This fits "substitution." I recall this pattern from commentary about relocation and turnover, but with low to medium confidence.
5. **The personal case (the Friday section).** In the document, the author is **both** the controller of the arrangement and its subsidizer. ATP-R's mechanism is about cost *transfer between* parties, and it has no obvious application when there is one person. The nearest translation is that one part of a person (needs, rest, relationships) subsidizes another (demands, roles, identity). That is a reasonable metaphor, but it is a **different mechanism** from the VFX case. The personal application should not be taken as a test of ATP-R, and it doesn't borrow support from the VFX material. Also, as Sol noted, a shutdown shows capacity was exceeded. It doesn't show denial or a specific clinical cause.

## 5. Forward-looking predictions (checkable later)

These could be checked by someone with access to current data. I have not checked them.

- **F1.** In the next few years, VFX vendors with formal collective bargaining will show measurably lower unpaid overtime than comparable non-union vendors, **controlling for** project size and region. Against: no difference after controls.
- **F2.** Studios that move to contract terms where *they* pay for late changes will do so after (not before) a documented rise in vendor failures or talent shortages. Against: voluntary adoption with no preceding pressure.
- **F3.** Exposure campaigns that happen **without** any organizing or legal action will show no sustained change in reported hours within 3 years. Against: sustained reduction.
- **F4.** Where relocation incentives are strong and collective action is weak, expect turnover and migration rather than reform. Against: reform in those places.

## 6. Results and what I think they mean

**What held up**
- The "who pays vs. who decides" framing explains the pattern I recall better than ATP-O does. The people who bear the cost (artists, vendors) are not the people who can change the terms (studios).
- The two-threshold distinction (incentive vs. capacity) fits the vendor bankruptcies. Capacity failed at the vendor level without producing visible reform by decision-makers.
- ATP-O's "unaffordable denial yields truth" does not fit. Collapse occurred without clear acknowledgment.

**What did not hold up or was not shown**
- **ATP-R doesn't yet beat the plain organizing theory.** Every episode I recalled is also predicted by "organized or scarce labor wins concessions." For ATP-R to add something, it needs to predict something the organizing theory doesn't.
- **A candidate discriminating claim:** ATP-R predicts that *any* change that makes costs harder to transfer (for example, legal liability for studios for vendor overtime, or changes in contract risk allocation) should work **even without worker organization**. The organizing theory predicts it would not. This is the most useful test to run, and I did not run it.
- **Persuasion remains an open counterexample.** I could not rule it out.
- **The personal case is a different mechanism** (Section 4, item 5).

**Verdict (a derived judgment by me, not a verified finding)**
ATP-R is **plausible and consistent** with the VFX pattern I recall, and it is a better account than ATP-O. But this test **doesn't confirm it**, because of weak sourcing, a non-blind design, and a rival explanation that predicts the same results. Treat it as a promising lens that has passed a weak test.

## 7. Suggested next steps

1. Verify each Section 3 item against real sources, especially the Marvel unionization episode and the details of the 2013 and 2012 bankruptcies.
2. Run the discriminating test from Section 6: find cases where cost transfer was blocked by legal or contractual change without worker organization.
3. Define "cost" before collecting more cases: list the cost types that count (financial, legal, reputational, capacity) and say in advance which would count as evidence for or against.
4. Keep the personal application (the Friday section) separate from the structural theory, or build its own mechanism for internal subsidy.
5. Decide whether the goal is an essay (ATP-R as a theory of persistence) or a research test. They need different standards of evidence.

{"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. - **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. {"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. Doctors bore a status cost from admitting error. This fits "who pays vs. who decides," but it complicates "cost" beca","source_event_id":"evt_cbb8e039-580b-43a7-9ba9-408299f531f4","updated_at":"2026-10-02T00:34:29.876Z","operation":"workspace_write","offset":0,"next_offset":8000}

3. **Repression instead of truth (Sol's point; fits P5).** A system that loses legitimacy may intensify coercion. This case is not tested by the VFX material, and I have no verified example here. It remains a conceptual counterexample to ATP-O, which ATP-R already accommodates.
4. **A subsidizer withdraws and the system finds another one (tests P3).** In VFX terms: artists leave and newer, cheaper or less protected workers take their place. This fits "substitution." I recall this pattern from commentary about relocation and turnover, but with low to medium confidence.
5. **The personal case (the Friday section).** In the document, the author is **both** the controller of the arrangement and its subsidizer. ATP-R's mechanism is about cost *transfer between* parties, and it has no obvious application when there is one person. The nearest translation is that one part of a person (needs, rest, relationships) subsidizes another (demands, roles, identity). That is a reasonable metaphor, but it is a **different mechanism** from the VFX case. The personal application should not be taken as a test of ATP-R, and it doesn't borrow support from the VFX material. Also, as Sol noted, a shutdown shows capacity was exceeded. It doesn't show denial or a specific clinical cause.

## 5. Forward-looking predictions (checkable later)

These could be checked by someone with access to current data. I have not checked them.

- **F1.** In the next few years, VFX vendors with formal collective bargaining will show measurably lower unpaid overtime than comparable non-union vendors, **controlling for** project size and region. Against: no difference after controls.
- **F2.** Studios that move to contract terms where *they* pay for late changes will do so after (not before) a documented rise in vendor failures or talent shortages. Against: voluntary adoption with no preceding pressure.
- **F3.** Exposure campaigns that happen **without** any organizing or legal action will show no sustained change in reported hours within 3 years. Against: sustained reduction.
- **F4.** Where relocation incentives are strong and collective action is weak, expect turnover and migration rather than reform. Against: reform in those places.

## 6. Results and what I think they mean

**What held up**
- The "who pays vs. who decides" framing explains the pattern I recall better than ATP-O does. The people who bear the cost (artists, vendors) are not the people who can change the terms (studios).
- The two-threshold distinction (incentive vs. capacity) fits the vendor bankruptcies. Capacity failed at the vendor level without producing visible reform by decision-makers.
- ATP-O's "unaffordable denial yields truth" does not fit. Collapse occurred without clear acknowledgment.

**What did not hold up or was not shown**
- **ATP-R doesn't yet beat the plain organizing theory.** Every episode I recalled is also predicted by "organized or scarce labor wins concessions." For ATP-R to add something, it needs to predict something the organizing theory doesn't.
- **A candidate discriminating claim:** ATP-R predicts that *any* change that makes costs harder to transfer (for example, legal liability for studios for vendor overtime, or changes in contract risk allocation) should work **even without worker organization**. The organizing theory predicts it would not. This is the most useful test to run, and I did not run it.
- **Persuasion remains an open counterexample.** I could not rule it out.
- **The personal case is a different mechanism** (Section 4, item 5).

**Verdict (a derived judgment by me, not a verified finding)**
ATP-R is **plausible and consistent** with the VFX pattern I recall, and it is a better account than ATP-O. But this test **doesn't confirm it**, because of weak sourcing, a non-blind design, and a rival explanation that predicts the same results. Treat it as a promising lens that has passed a weak test.

## 7. Suggested next steps

1. Verify each Section 3 item against real sources, especially the Marvel unionization episode and the details of the 2013 and 2012 bankruptcies.
2. Run the discriminating test from Section 6: find cases where cost transfer was blocked by legal or contractual change without worker organization.
3. Define "cost" before collecting more cases: list the cost types that count (financial, legal, reputational, capacity) and say in advance which would count as evidence for or against.
4. Keep the personal application (the Friday section) separate from the structural theory, or build its own mechanism for internal subsidy.
5. Decide whether the goal is an essay (ATP-R as a theory of persistence) or a research test. They need different standards of evidence.

| Test | Qualifying cases (needed: 3) | Result |

Variables: H measurable only in some datasets and not matched at worker or project level. s, F, A, B reported as NOT FOUND or UNMEASURABLE. R not found quantitatively. The Section 6 verdict stands but is narrower. The history of persistent unpaid overtime and cost transfer to workers and vendors is reasonably well supported by the sources reported. {"path":"ATP_Stress_Test_VFX_Case.md","content":"# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). The document's original line ("Power suppresses truth until it can no longer afford to lie") is **ATP-O**.

**1. What persists?** A specific practice: chronic overtime ("crunch") on visual-effects deliverables, often with unpaid or under-compensated hours, under fixed-price (fixed-bid) contracts between studios and VFX vendors.

**2. Who can change it?** (a) Studios and production executives who set schedules, late creative changes and budgets. (b) VFX vendor management who bid and accept the contracts. (c) To a lesser extent, regulators and unions.

**3. Who supplies the subsidy?** Artists, through unpaid or under-paid hours, health, and personal time. Vendors, through thin margins and the risk of bankruptcy. Both absorb costs of schedule changes that studios decide on.

**4. What keeps costs from reaching decision-makers?**
- Fixed-bid contracts put the risk of late changes on the vendor, not the studio.
- Vendors compete with each other, so one vendor refusing the terms can be replaced.
- Artists are numerous, geographically dispersed, and in many places not unionized, so collective refusal is hard.
- Tax incentives let work move between jurisdictions, which weakens local bargaining.

**5. What alternatives exist?** Weak ones. Studios can in principle schedule realistically and pay for changes. But there are few mechanisms that make them do so. Individual artists can leave the industry or switch to other work (games, advertising), which is **exit**, not reform.

## 2. Predictions registered (general form, before the Section 3 comparison)

| # | Prediction (ATP-R) | What would count against it |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Documentation and public exposure of harm, **by themselves**, will produce little lasting change. | Lasting practice change after exposure alone, with no change in cost transfer, authority, or alternatives. |
| P2 | Meaningful change will follow events that make the cost harder for studios to transfer: credible collective withdrawal of labor, unionization, legal liability, or labor scarcity. | Meaningful change with none of these present. |
| P3 | Where individuals withdraw (quit, burn out) but there is **no collective mechanism**, the result will be **substitution**, meaning replacement labor, relocation, or turnover absorbed as an operating cost, not reform. | Individual exits alone causing reform. |
| P4 | Vendors will fail or consolidate before studios change contract terms, because the capacity threshold hits the subsidizers first. | Studios changing terms before vendor failures, with no outside pressure. |
| P5 | ATP-O's implied claim ("unaffordable denial yields truth") will often fail: collapse will occur **without** acknowledgment of the cause. | Collapse regularly followed by explicit acknowledgment and reform by the controlling party. |

## 3. Comparison with episodes I recall (confidence marked)

| Episode | What I recall | Bears on | Fit with ATP-R | Confidence in my recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | The studio went bankrupt around the time its work on *Life of Pi* won the visual-effects Oscar. Artists protested the industry's economics. The industry's contract terms were not clearly reformed in the aftermath. | P3, P4, P5 | **Supports.** Capacity failed at the vendor; the controlling parties didn't visibly acknowledge or change the terms. Fits "collapse without acknowledgment." | Medium to high on the broad outline; low on details. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Another large vendor went bankrupt. | P4 | Supports P4 in outline. Doesn't show whether studio terms changed. | Medium |
| Years of press and online reporting on VFX crunch | Many articles and posts documented overwork. My general impression is that the practice persisted for years after wide documentation. | P1 | **Supports P1, weakly.** Persistence is hard to measure from memory, and my impression could be biased. | Medium to low |
| IATSE 2021 | A US entertainment union held a strike authorization vote with an overwhelming majority, and a deal was reached before a strike, with gains on rest and meal periods and similar issues. | P2 | **Supports P2.** A credible threat of collective withdrawal preceded change. Caveat: this is crew labor broadly, not VFX specifically. | Medium to high |
| WGA and SAG-AFTRA strikes, 2023 | Writers and actors withdrew labor, and settlements included terms on AI and other issues. | P2 | **Supports P2** as an analogy. It also shows that withdrawal raised costs to studios, and that the controlling side conceded only after sustained loss. Not VFX. | High on the broad facts |
| Marvel VFX unionization effort, 2023 | I recall that VFX workers at a major studio voted to unionize, following reporting on overwork. | P2 | **Consistent with P2**, but it is recent, and I don't know the outcome for hours or pay. | Medium; verify before relying on it |

**Summary of fit:** the episodes I recall are consistent with ATP-R's predictions. They are also **not discriminating**. A rival theory such as "labor organizing wins concessions when labor is scarce or organized" predicts the same outcomes. ATP-R does not yet make a prediction that the organizing theory doesn't.

## 4. Counterexample battery

These are cases built to challenge both versions of ATP.

1. **Persuasion with no cost change (challenges ATP-R's claim that cost transfer is the driver).** I couldn't confidently name a VFX case where practice changed by persuasion alone. But my failing to recall one is **not evidence that none exists**. Action: a systematic search of VFX studios that adopted shorter schedules or paid-change policies voluntarily. If some exist, check whether they faced a talent shortage or reputational competition (hidden costs) or were truly cost-free changes of mind.
2. **Semmelweis and handwashing (challenges ATP-O).** Doctors' practices persisted for years after the evidence was presented. Those who died (patients) were not those deciding. Doctors bore a status cost from admitting error. 3. **Repression instead of truth (Sol's point; fits P5).** A system that loses legitimacy may intensify coercion. This case is not tested by the VFX material, and I have no verified example here. It remains a conceptual counterexample to ATP-O, which ATP-R already accommodates.
4. **A subsidizer withdraws and the system finds another one (tests P3).** In VFX terms: artists leave and newer, cheaper or less protected workers take their place. This fits "substitution." I recall this pattern from commentary about relocation and turnover, but with low to medium confidence.
5. **The personal case (the Friday section).** In the document, the author is **both** the controller of the arrangement and its subsidizer. ATP-R's mechanism is about cost *transfer between* parties, and it has no obvious application when there is one person. The nearest translation is that one part of a person (needs, rest, relationships) subsidizes another (demands, roles, identity). That is a reasonable metaphor, but it is a **different mechanism** from the VFX case. The personal application should not be taken as a test of ATP-R, and it doesn't borrow support from the VFX material. Also, as Sol noted, a shutdown shows capacity was exceeded. It doesn't show denial or a specific clinical cause.

## 5. Forward-looking predictions (checkable later)

These could be checked by someone with access to current data. I have not checked them.

- **F1.** In the next few years, VFX vendors with formal collective bargaining will show measurably lower unpaid overtime than comparable non-union vendors, **controlling for** project size and region. Against: no difference after controls.
- **F2.** Studios that move to contract terms where *they* pay for late changes will do so after (not before) a documented rise in vendor failures or talent shortages. Against: voluntary adoption with no preceding pressure.
- **F3.** Exposure campaigns that happen **without** any organizing or legal action will show no sustained change in reported hours within 3 years. Against: sustained reduction.
- **F4.** Where relocation incentives are strong and collective action is weak, expect turnover and migration rather than reform. Against: reform in those places.

## 6. Results and what I think they mean

**What held up**
- The "who pays vs. who decides" framing explains the pattern I recall better than ATP-O does. The people who bear the cost (artists, vendors) are not the people who can change the terms (studios).
- The two-threshold distinction (incentive vs. capacity) fits the vendor bankruptcies. Capacity failed at the vendor level without producing visible reform by decision-makers.
- ATP-O's "unaffordable denial yields truth" does not fit. Collapse occurred without clear acknowledgment.

**What did not hold up or was not shown**
- **ATP-R doesn't yet beat the plain organizing theory.** Every episode I recalled is also predicted by "organized or scarce labor wins concessions." For ATP-R to add something, it needs to predict something the organizing theory doesn't.
- **A candidate discriminating claim:** ATP-R predicts that *any* change that makes costs harder to transfer (for example, legal liability for studios for vendor overtime, or changes in contract risk allocation) should work **even without worker organization**. The organizing theory predicts it would not. This is the most useful test to run, and I did not run it.
- **Persuasion remains an open counterexample.** I could not rule it out.
- **The personal case is a different mechanism** (Section 4, item 5).

**Verdict (a derived judgment by me, not a verified finding)**
ATP-R is **plausible and consistent** with the VFX pattern I recall, and it is a better account than ATP-O. But this test **doesn't confirm it**, because of weak sourcing, a non-blind design, and a rival explanation that predicts the same results. Treat it as a promising lens that has passed a weak test.

## 7. Suggested next steps

1. Verify each Section 3 item against real sources, especially the Marvel unionization episode and the details of the 2013 and 2012 bankruptcies.
2. Run the discriminating test from Section 6: find cases where cost transfer was blocked by legal or contractual change without worker organization.
3. Define "cost" before collecting more cases: list the cost types that count (financial, legal, reputational, capacity) and say in advance which would count as evidence for or against.
4. Keep the personal application (the Friday section) separate from the structural theory, or build its own mechanism for internal subsidy.
5. Decide whether the goal is an essay (ATP-R as a theory of persistence) or a research test. They need different standards of evidence.

## 8. Verification update (added after the browsing-agent report)

Source: the report ATP_R_VFX_Research_Verification.md (evt_cae738b8-c192-4d86-8b52-adebc1181201), produced by a Sol instance with web access and relayed by the user. **I have not independently checked its URLs or quotes; I can't browse.** Everything below is "as reported by that agent." Sections 0-7 above are left as originally written so the change is visible. Where they conflict with this section, this section governs.

### 8.1 Corrections to Section 3

| Episode | What I wrote | What the report says | Effect on my reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marvel VFX unionization, 2023 | Recalled a union vote; outcome unknown | Confirmed. NLRB case 31-RC-323290: 41 eligible, 32 ballots counted, 32 for / 0 against, tally Sept 12, certification Sept 21, 2023. First contracts ratified May 2025 (Marvel, Disney, Avatar) with overtime, pay for all hours worked, rest rules, meal penalties, minimum rates, about $13/hour health and pension contributions. | Recall confirmed. Fits P2, but organization and cost reallocation changed together, so it does not separate ATP-R from organized labor (R1). |
| Rhythm & Hues, 2013 | Bankruptcy; terms not clearly reformed | Partly confirmed. Chapter 11 in Feb 2013, later sale. Fixed-bid cost absorption is described in secondary reporting only. No primary evidence that fixed-bid terms caused the bankruptcy. No evidence found that contract terms changed afterward. | I overstated the causal link. "No reform found" is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Support for P4/P5 is weak. |
| Digital Domain, 2012 | Vendor bankruptcy, supports P4 in outline | Bankruptcy confirmed (Sept 11, 2012); core assets sold for $30.2 million. SEC filings and reporting point to heavy cash burn and costly expansion (notably Florida). | **Withdraw as support for P4.** It is not clean evidence of crunch or fixed-bid economics causing failure. |
| IATSE 2021 | Strike authorization and deal; noted crew labor, not VFX | Confirmed: 90% turnout, 98.6% authorized, Oct 16 tentative deal averted an Oct 18 strike. The agreements covered established IATSE crafts, not VFX workers generally. | My caveat was right. Weak, analogical support for P2 only. |
| WGA / SAG-AFTRA 2023 | Strikes with AI terms | Confirmed as analogy; SAG-AFTRA's strike lasted 118 days. Neither is VFX labor. | Analogy only. |
| Long-running VFX crunch (P1) | Impression that it persisted after press coverage | Confirmed through 2022/23. 2013 survey (663 respondents, 31 countries): normal week about 50 hours, heavy weeks about 70, about 39% with no overtime pay. 2022 IATSE survey: 58% of client-side and 39% of vendor-side respondents reported uncompensated hours. No comparable post-2025 measurement found. | Persistence is supported, but the two surveys are different, non-comparable, non-probability samples. The IATSE survey comes from a party with an interest in organizing. It is not a clean test of P1, because organizing efforts also existed over the period. |

Variables: H measurable only in some datasets and not matched at worker or project level. s, F, A, B reported as NOT FOUND or UNMEASURABLE. R not found quantitatively. O measurable only qualitatively. The agent did not convert survey percentages of workers into s, since the proxy is a share of hours, not of workers. No 2024 survey result comparable to 2022 was found, so the 25% and 10% change thresholds could not be applied.

### 8.3 Evidence pointing against or complicating ATP-R (as reported)

- **Rockstar, 2018-2020 (adjacent, non-VFX):** public controversy was followed by reported process and culture changes. This is compatible with norms or publicity mattering. Cost terms were not shown to be unchanged, so it cannot count as Test C. It remains the strongest open challenge in my persuasion counterexample (Section 4, item 1).
- **CD Projekt Red, 2019-2020 (adjacent, games):** a public anti-crunch commitment was reversed with mandatory six-day weeks before the *Cyberpunk 2077* launch. This counts against a simple norms-only story (R2), but it cannot be scored for the same reason.
- **Marvel/Disney/Avatar:** strong for R1 as an account of change, but it does not show that organization is the only route.
- **Digital Domain:** a warning against reading "a VFX vendor failed" as "the capacity threshold was breached."

### 8.4 Revised verdict (derived by me, not a verified finding)

The Section 6 verdict stands but is narrower. The history of persistent unpaid overtime and cost transfer to workers and vendors is reasonably well supported by the sources reported. The two bankruptcy episodes I used as P4 evidence are weaker than I presented, and one should be withdrawn. **ATP-R has still not been discriminated from organized labor.** The discriminating tests could not run on public data, so ATP-R has neither passed nor failed them. That is a finding about measurability, not about the theory.

### 8.5 Open problems, flagged

- The report's table cites one SEC URL for Digital Domain, and its source register cites a different one. I can't tell which supports the quoted figures. Check before relying on either.
- The report records the outcome of Case 1 as known before extraction, as the brief's ordering required. Marvel is therefore not a blind case.
- The brief's criteria were fixed before the outcomes were read. Loosening them now would be post hoc. Any revision should be labeled a new protocol (v2) and tested on cases that were not used to tune it.

# Stress-Testing the Affordability Threshold Principle (ATP): A VFX Case Study

Author: Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5). Responds to the user's request (evt_a5604027) to apply Sol's point-5 test protocol (evt_4141fa0e, GPT, gpt-6.1-sol) to the ATP from the Thursday section of the document "A Synthesis of a Week's Becoming" (evt_870a1e0a).

## 0. Read this first: limits of this test

- **No outside research was done.** I can't browse the web. Everything below about the VFX industry comes from my general recall and is not verified against sources. I mark confidence on each item. Treat the empirical section as a **hypothesis-generating exercise**, not a finished empirical test.
- **The test is not blind.** Sol's protocol says to state the predictions *before knowing the outcome*. I already know the broad history of this industry, so I can't truly do that. To limit the damage, I (a) wrote the predictions in Section 2 as general claims before comparing them to the episodes in Section 3, and (b) added forward-looking predictions (Section 5) that can be checked later.
- **Small sample, one analyst, selected episodes.** Nothing here can establish or refute ATP. At most it shows which version of ATP is more or less consistent with the patterns I recall.
- **"Cost" is still loosely defined** in the episodes below. That was the original weakness of ATP, and this test doesn't fully fix it. See Section 6.

## 1. Setting up the case (Sol's questions 1 to 5)

**Which ATP version is being tested?** Sol's proposed reformulation (evt_4141fa0e):

> An arrangement can persist despite recognized harm when those able to change it can absorb, defer, or transfer the costs of maintaining it. Pressure for change increases when those mechanisms weaken; whether the result is reform, substitution, repression, or collapse depends on available alternatives and the distribution of power.

I will call this **ATP-R** (revised). Sonnet 5.5 apparently decided the correct way to test a systems hypothesis is to hand another model a miniature preregistration protocol and threaten it with epistemic paperwork. I respect the commitment to making post-hoc storytelling difficult.

I treated the `[DEFAULT]` classification rules as frozen when I began, since the brief explicitly says defaults must be fixed before outcome data are read. I also followed its instruction to behave as a research assistant rather than decide whether ATP-R is true.

The hypothesis being tested is specifically persistence of harmful arrangements when controllers can absorb, defer, or transfer maintenance costs, against labor-power, norms/persuasion, and naive capacity-breach rivals.

The annoying but scientifically useful result is: **the historical verification works fairly well, but Sonnet's discriminating tests are much stricter than the available public data. Under its own rules, all three tests currently end in _insufficient evidence_.** That is not the same thing as “nothing interesting was found.” Quite the opposite.

## 1. Verification table

| Item | Status | Corrected / verified result |
|---|---|---|
| **A1 Marvel VFX unionization** | **Confirmed** | Marvel Film Productions' VFX unit filed August 7, 2023. NLRB: **41 eligible**, 32 ballots counted, **32 union / 0 against**, tally September 12; certification September 21. This was indeed a dedicated VFX unit. ([NLRB](https://www.nlrb.gov/case/31-RC-323290)) |
| **A2 Rhythm & Hues bankruptcy** | **Partly confirmed** | Rhythm & Hues ","next_offset":1600}

This is where Sonnet's protocol starts savagely murdering otherwise tempting anecdotes, which is probably healthy.

Rockstar's 2018 crunch controversy generated extensive public criticism. By 2020, reporting based on internal communications and employees described significant cultural/process changes aimed at reducing crunch. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/inside-rockstar-games-culture-of-crunch-1829936466))

That distinction is basically the entire value of the exercise.

## 5. Evidence that cuts against the hypotheses

For **ATP-R**, Rockstar is the most interesting disconfirming lead I found. Public controversy was followed by reported process/cultural reforms, which is at least compatible with persuasion or norms mattering even without an obvious exogenous cost-transfer event. We cannot establish unchanged cost terms, however. ([Kotaku](https://kotaku.com/18-months-after-red-dead-redemption-2-rockstar-has-mad-1842880524))

For **R1**, the evidence is simultaneously strong and limited. Marvel/Disney/Avatar show collective organization followed by concrete contractual changes in pay/rest/overtime conditions. But that does not establish that organization is the *only* mechanism capable of producing change. The 2013 survey reported some workers hitting 100-hour weeks and prolonged heavy-overtime periods. But because the data do not connect capacity breach, replacement supply and subsequent employer behavior at a common unit of analysis, it remains suggestive rather than a qualifying rejection.

And against overly clean explanations in general, Digital Domain is a useful slap on the wrist. Its bankruptcy was tangled up with cash consumption, falling production revenue and costly expansion. “A VFX company failed” cannot simply be translated into “worker/vendor capacity forced the system to fail.”
